comparison: Both strongly support the spatial findings (C3, C4, C13, C64) regarding sensory representations in somatosensory cortex and perceptual representations in visual regions. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical testing and experimental design; peer reviewers describe evidence as 'convincing.' OpenEval also includes C5 (LOC as hinge region) which peer reviewers address separately.

Both address C5 and C19 regarding LOC as a 'hinge' region. OpenEval rates C19 as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting it is labeled as speculation by authors and not directly tested. Peer reviewers rate both claims as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 explicitly affirming LOC's pivotal role without expressing reservations about the speculative nature.

Perfect agreement on temporal findings (C6, C7, C8, C65). Both rate as SUPPORTED with strong affirmation of sequential emergence of sensory before perceptual representations. OpenEval notes the 50-timepoint criterion is somewhat arbitrary; peer reviewers describe evidence as 'convincing' without methodological concerns.

Both address fMRI RSA behavioral relevance (C9, C10, C44). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with acknowledgment of task-dependence; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 explicitly noting 'conclusions regarding behavioral relevance...are limited due to the behavioral measurements adopted.' This represents a substantive disagreement on interpretation strength.

Both address EEG RSA behavioral relevance (C45, C46, C72, C73). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but notes wide confidence intervals and marginal significance; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, applying the same behavioral measurement limitations noted for fMRI RSA. OpenEval is more accepting despite noting uncertainty; peer reviewers more cautious.

Both strongly support perceptual representations in visual regions (C14, C17, C18, C76). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but notes 'modality-independent' interpretation goes beyond direct demonstration; peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED with Reviewer 2 calling evidence 'convincing' and noting findings in LOC, VWFA, and EVC as strengths.

Both support sensory representations in somatosensory regions (C20, C21, C22, C53). OpenEval and peer reviewers both rate SUPPORTED with consistent interpretation of functional properties. No substantive disagreements on these claims.

Both address EEG searchlight findings (C66, C67, C68). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 noting 'ROI and searchlight analyses are not completely overlapping,' suggesting some discrepancy. OpenEval does not identify this as a concern, representing a difference in evaluation.

Both address TMS comparison and behavioral utilization (C32, C33). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting strong causal inference goes beyond correlation and TMS study was in sighted readers; peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED without challenging the interpretation. This represents disagreement on the strength of causal claims.

Both address temporal comparison with visual processing and braille efficiency (C26, C27, C28, C31). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but notes C31 is speculative without direct testing; peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED without expressing reservations. OpenEval includes additional claims (C29, C30) not explicitly addressed by peer reviewers.

Both address sequential processing principle (C57, C25, C60). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting temporal sequence is well-demonstrated; peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED with Reviewer 1 explicitly affirming the sensory-to-cognitive progression pattern. Strong agreement on this interpretive conclusion. Peer result also includes C58, C59 which OpenEval addresses separately.

Both address summary conclusions (C58, C59). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as appropriate high-level interpretations; peer reviewers also affirm these conclusions within their broader discussion of the sequential processing principle. Strong agreement on main conclusions.

Both address methodological claims (C34-C43, with OpenEval also including C71). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but notes concern about partial sample overlap between fMRI and EEG; peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 calling it 'very well-designed' without noting the overlap concern. Minor difference in methodological scrutiny.

Both address background/contextual claims (C1, C2, C11, C12). Both rate SUPPORTED as appropriate context and motivation. These are not novel findings but establish the study framework. Complete agreement.

OpenEval addresses reorganization vs. capacity-based accounts (C47-C51) and rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the study does not directly test between theoretical accounts. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these theoretical interpretation claims.

OpenEval addresses connectivity and information flow speculation (C54-C56) and rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these architectural claims.

OpenEval addresses multimodal terminology (C52) and rates as SUPPORTED but suggests 'supramodal' or 'amodal' would be more precise than 'multimodal' for blind participants. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this terminological issue.

OpenEval addresses operational definitions of sensory vs. perceptual (C62, C63) and rates as SUPPORTED, noting the within-hand vs. across-hand scheme is reasonable but represents a proxy measure. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these definitional claims.

OpenEval addresses limitations of activation-based studies and RSA justification (C61, C69, C70, C74, C75) and rates as SUPPORTED as accurate characterization of prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these methodological context claims.

OpenEval addresses various literature citations (C15, C16, C21-C24) and rates as SUPPORTED as accurate representation of prior findings. Peer reviewers address some overlapping claims (C21, C22) within R7 but not as a distinct evaluation of the literature review.
